hook_text: Jobs data can't predict anything — and economists know it. Here's the bus that explains why.
clip_script: Put the economy in a minibus running the N3 from Durban to Johannesburg at night. The driver reads three kinds of information, and so does a country. Headlights light up the road ahead: building plans approved, job adverts published, orders placed with factories. Each one is a promise about next year — nobody orders parts for a factory they intend to close. Leading indicators. The speedometer reads this instant: tills ringing, factories producing, GDP itself. Coincident indicators. And the rear-view mirror — here's the surprise — holds JOBS. Think like an employer. When business sours, you hold on to staff, hoping the dip passes. When business improves, you wait to hire until you are certain. Either way, employment moves LAST. By the time unemployment finally falls, the recovery is already old. Lagging indicators confirm the past; they never announce the future. Two habits finish the licence: never confuse the size of the bus with its speed — and never trust a reading in rands without asking what prices did. Rands stretch in the heat. Kilometres do not.
visual_style: A minibus dashboard at night: headlight beams revealing tiny building plans and job adverts, a speedometer needle labelled GDP, and a rear-view mirror where the word JOBS trails behind the bus; a final split showing a stretching rand note beside a rigid kilometre marker.
pacing: Three quick beats for the three instruments, a pause on the jobs-in-the-mirror reveal, brisk close on the two habits.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any economics headline knowing exactly which instrument it came from.
